rows.raw: " [var0 |You ask Zo if she’s willing to swords-dance with you again. Being able to move so fluidly with a sword has some advantages that you would never have guessed before you practiced with her, and you’d like to keep yourself keen. |You’d never guess it from the way she carries herself, or the way she dresses, but Zo is a wonderful dancer, and she uses the most unusual of props with her movements: while you could see a dancer move with a cane, or a pole, and you’ve even heard of dancers playing with fire, you’ve never seen anyone dance with a sword and scabbard like she does. You ask Zo if she’s willing to try and teach you to dance like that – or, at least, if she’s willing to dance like that for you. ] [flags.ZO_BAB_RANDO |Zo nods once, hefting Vai into her arms and taking him into the [flags.ZO_UPGRADE 3|house|shack] to put him to bed for the time being. Although you and Zo are masters at what you two do, it’s nonetheless safer that your baby isn’t in the presence of you whipping around weapons for the sake of your training, no matter how confident you two are. When she emerges, Vai is gone, and in his place is Zo’s sword, still in its scabbard, gripped just beneath where the sword’s cross guard meets the sheath. Once she gets back to the grassy field, she bows, but doesn’t give you the blade; instead, she unsheathes it herself: the sword’s edge grinds sharply against the reinforced skeleton of the scabbard, and the flawless, untainted steel of the blade glints in the sunlight. |Zo nods once and gently grips you by the wrist, pulling you towards the empty, grassy field towards the back of her grove. [var1 |She already has the sword and the scabbard in her possession: she sheathes it, then bows before you, with the weapon spread across both of her open palms, before she unsheathes it again, the flawless, untainted steel of the blade glinting in the sunlight as its edge grinds against the reinforced skeleton of the scabbard. Perhaps that was all for courtesy? |Once you’re there, she points to you, then points down to the grass, then points up to the sky, and turns and leaves for her shanty to retrieve her sword. Once she returns, she stands in front of you with the sword, still sheathed in its scabbard, across both her upturned palms. Once she gets back to the grassy field, she bows, but doesn’t give you the blade; instead, she unsheathes it herself: the sword’s edge grinds sharply against the reinforced skeleton of the scabbard, and the flawless, untainted steel of the blade glints in the sunlight. ] ] [zo.equanimityRange 0 1 2 3 |She hands you the scabbard with her left hand, and turns the sword into a reverse grip in her right. She’s not going to trust you with the sword on your first lesson. That would be foolish. Once you have it, she holds out her occupied hand, the sword held perpendicular to the ground, in her reverse grip, her palm facing upward; she thrusts her fist a few times, motioning for you to mimic her stance. You do, and already the sensation feels alien to you: the scabbard is weighted similarly to a sword, in that it’s heavy all throughout and the elongated end tries to pull your wrist down to the ground. Holding it in a reverse grip tenses different muscles in your wrist, too – it’s only been a moment and it already feels more strenuous on your hand to hold the scabbard so unnaturally. It’s difficult for Zo to not notice that you’re having such a difficult time with holding the scabbard. Despite your conscious attempts to keep it steady, she’s the type of person that can notice the smallest of things, and your wrist being a bit shaky with the sheath is probably clear as could be to her. Still, she smiles patiently, waiting for you to tell her that you’re ready to continue. When you do, she demonstrates a simple trick: she flicks her wrist forward and releases her grip on her sword as she twists her hand, her palm facing downward. The sword, drawn by the momentum, spins once, the blade of the sword swishing through the air diagonally, the tip swinging close enough to her face to make you flinch, but she barely reacts to it. Once the sword makes a single, full rotation, she grabs it again and motions to you, to replicate what she just did. You look at your hand, palm-side facing up, the scabbard clenched in your fingers. It shouldn’t be too hard, should it? One little twirl? You lean the scabbard backward a bit, before you fling the weighted scabbard forward in your hand and you release your grip– And the whole thing flies forward, spinning harmlessly through the air in front of you, hitting the grass with a soft thud. You didn’t even make it halfway. Zo laughs to herself, her chest heaving with her breath and her eyes shut into crescents, although no sound escapes her throat. She retrieves the scabbard for you, plucking it from the grass with her free hand, and presenting it to you again. When you reassume the grip, she pushes down on your wrist, realigning your balance, and pulls gently on your fingers, telling you to lighten your grip slightly before the spin. Then, she steps back and lets you try again. You spin it again– And you whap yourself right in the shoulder with the end of the scabbard, before it falls to the grass at your feet. But you made progress that time! |She hands you the scabbard with her left hand, and turns the sword into a reverse grip in her right. You made some decent progress with her last lesson, and you even managed to complete a single twirl with the scabbard, but she isn’t quite ready to trust you with the sword yet. Not that you blame her. This time, Zo holds the sword upright, the blade pinched between her thumb and index finger just above the sword’s wrist guard with her other hand pressed behind her back. You know that the sword is sharp, so the way she’s pinching it gives you some pause: if she slips, it’ll damn-near cut her thumb off. But, even though it’s just her two fingers, the blade is held sturdy and upright, waiting unflinchingly for you to mimic her grip. Once you do, Zo flicks her wrist forward and releases her grip on the sword. The handle swings outward, away from her, and the bladed end comes swinging down onto her shoulder; you flinch for her when the gleaming metal of the sword hits her arm, but the motion of the flick had twisted the blade so its broad end came down on her sleeve instead. Fluidly, she lifts her arm upward, starting at her wrist, then her elbow, to continue the sword on its forward-rolling motion, until the tip of the blade lifts off her sleeve, tracing along the fabric of her suit, it traces along her fingers, where she catches it again, pinched once more between her thumb and index finger. She doesn’t bother completing a second loop: you probably get the picture, but she nonetheless lowers the blade gently until she can grip onto its handle. Then, with her patient smile turning her eyes into crescents beneath her silver mask, she motions to you, allowing you to have your turn. The scabbard isn’t even a little sharp, taking away one of the scarier aspects of performing the same trick, but it’s still heavy, and if you accidentally reflect the motion of the scabbard into your arm instead of absorbing it, it’s probably going to leave a bit of a bruise. You try to mentally plan out the motion of the scabbard; the momentum it’s going to have with its weight as it comes down; the motion your arm will have to take in order to absorb its weight... and, not to forget, you have to bounce it back upward so that you can catch the opposite end of the scabbard between your fingers again. Once you’re ready, after a breath, you flick your wrist backward, sending the scabbard down onto your arm. You follow its motion, sinking your arm just as it bears down on you, absorbing the motion into you rather than reflecting it. So far so– When you try to bounce it back upward, you don’t put in enough force, and you accidentally readjust your arm. The scabbard bounces almost straight up, then, its open end hits you square on the arm before bouncing onto the grass below. If that had been the sword, that would have been its pointed tip skewering into you. You rub at the spot that the scabbard had hit you, soothing the sudden, dull pain there. You had gotten so close; it’s frustrating that you managed to get halfway on the first try, but you couldn’t clinch out the whole thing. Zo, though, has the opposite reaction: she has her hand on your other shoulder, and she’s enthusiastically smiling and nodding at you, positively enforcing your progress – she can’t exactly confirm, but you’re given the impression that you had surpassed her expectations on your first go. You may not have succeeded, but that doesn’t mean you did poorly. Zo stands beside you to pick up the scabbard for you, and once it’s between your fingers again, she slowly demonstrates the motion your arm should take with her own: you had gotten the first half down, but on the second, you jerked your arm suddenly and sharply. By her demonstration, you learn to keep the fluidity of your motion steady all throughout: to let the scabbard recoil through its own motion by moving with it, rather than to force it. She steps back, giving you space to try again. |By now, you’ve proven yourself at least somewhat proficient with swords-dancing – not even halfway to the degree that she is, but well enough that you can get your twirls and your bounces in with some fluidity and without a risk of hurting yourself too badly. Without any hesitation, Zo hands you the sword, the blade pointed down at the ground, keeping the scabbard for herself. You’re a bit apprehensive about taking the blade, but your teacher has unwavering faith that you can accomplish your next dance. Perhaps all you need is a bit of self-confidence... and to remember what you’ve learned so far, about keeping calm and level. Zo holds the scabbard in a reverse grip: her unoccupied left hand is balled into a fist and pressed against her right, looking as if she’s punching forward with both fists at once. She lifts the blade counterclockwise, then lets it fall, releasing her grip on all her fingers except her smallest; with its momentum, she twists the scabbard in between all eight of her fingers as it moves, swinging it in front of herself like a great, heavy fan, twisting it top-over-bottom over and over until it finally comes to the small finger in her left hand, where she catches it and holds it still, ending the scabbard’s journey in a reverse grip in her left hand. [var2] As difficult as that looked, you figure that that might actually be a bit easier with the sword: the grip of the sword is thinner than the scabbard, meaning it’ll be easier to pass finger-to-finger. Still, this is a real, sharpened blade in your hands: if you lose control while it’s on the upswing, the danger of it coming down on your wrists is very real. You keep what you had learned from your previous lessons on swords-dancing in mind as you lift the blade in a reverse grip. By this point, your muscles don’t nearly strain as hard to keep it aloft. The most important things to keep in mind are to let the sword move as it naturally wants to, with the momentum of the blade swinging top-over-bottom as it moves between your fingers, and to not force it to move in any particular direction. And the second-most important thing is to remain calm. There’s a state of equanimity that you need to achieve while you’re dancing with a blade: the way it moves, the way its edge sings as it cuts through the air, is not unlike you circling your lips and whistling. The sword isn’t a wild creature: it’s an extension of yourself. It moves the way it does because you have bid it to; if it doesn’t move the way you expect it to, that’s because of you, not because of it. You look down at your hands. The sword sits in your left hand, in reverse grip. You’ve already completed the task, on your first try, without any conscious input. You don’t remember doing it at all; the only physical reminder that it even happened is that your fingers feel a bit stretched. Zo approaches you with a knowing, caring smile, and she slides the scabbard onto the blade until it clicks into place, fully sheathing the sword. With both of her hands free, she holds you by both of your wrists, and she leans in to press her nose to yours as her eyes close in contentment. It’s a proud, sobering moment for you both: you have learned all you need to swords-dance like she can, and she’s taught you all she can. You have succeeded as her student, and she has succeeded as your teacher. |By now, you’ve proven yourself at least somewhat proficient with swords-dancing – not even halfway to the degree that she is, but well enough that you can get your twirls and your bounces in with some fluidity and without a risk of hurting yourself too badly. With both of her hands free, she holds you by both of your wrists, and she leans in to press her nose to yours as her eyes close in contentment. It’s a proud, sobering moment for you both: you have learned all you need to swords-dance like she can, and she’s taught you all she can. You have succeeded as her student, and she has succeeded as your teacher. ] "

rows.original: [zo.equanimityRange 0 1 2 3 |After about an hour’s worth of twirling the scabbard around in your hand, [pc.isDK |you start to get frustrated at it all, and you’re damn near about to call the whole thing a waste of time. Why bother owning a sword if you’re just going to perform silly dance moves with it? That’s not what a sword is for. |it’s... easy to begin to feel a bit distraught from your progress. All you have to show for your efforts are a bunch of bruises and the feeling that you might be wasting your time. It’s not like you’re going to go into battle twirling a sword in your fingers. ] Zo, recognizing your frustration, steps into your space and gently grabs the opposite end of the scabbard, lowering it, but not taking it from you. Looking into your eyes, she brings her free hand up to her chest, and takes a long, deep breath, in through her nose, and then waits a moment before exhaling, motioning to you as she does. You do as she implicitly instructs: a long, deep breath, in through your nose, and out through your mouth. You didn’t mean to come off as angry – you’re just... frazzled, is all. You just want to spin the damn thing across your hands. She could do it so easily. But then... she’s also been doing this for years. Still, the deep breath has the immediate effect of unwinding the tension you didn’t realize you had been building up in your shoulders. Zo lets go of the scabbard, then lifts her index finger. One more spin. Then, she steps back and lets you do it. You look to the scabbard in your hand, still held in a reverse grip. It’s been getting easier to hold it since you started. On some flicks, you spin too quickly; on some others, the angle of your arm is too steep. It’s all about striking a balance. You do as she wants, and spin it one last time. The scabbard swings across the back of your hand, its tip swishing through the air in front of your face, before flipping right-side-up again. You flip your wrist over to catch it– And you do! You nearly fumble it out of your fingers as you do, but you succeed! It took you an hour to make one single twirl, but, with that one victory, you feel like it was all worth it. Zo steps into your space again, her hands going to your shoulders this time, giving each of them a squeeze. Her eyes turn into crescents beneath her mask as she smiles beamingly at you. This was as much a victory for her as it was for you – her teaching methods are working. She extends her hand for you to place the scabbard into. That’s enough training for one day. |It’s hardly an easy swords-dancing routine to perform, but you nonetheless have a much easier time with it than the routine you had done before. You attribute that to a better understanding of what it is that Zo has been trying to teach you: it may seem like silly sword tricks that have no bearing or purpose in combat – and, well, it is and they don’t, but what she’s teaching you is to better understand how to move and coordinate yourself with a sword in your hand. The blade is as much an extension of yourself as it is a weapon or a tool, and the better, more dexterously, and more fluidly you can move with it in practice, the better you can wield it in combat. It takes a handful more tries (and a handful more aches and bruises), but eventually, you complete a single rotation of the scabbard moving against your arm, like she had demonstrated with the sword. A simple, single flip, and it’s pinched between your thumb and index finger once more. But, even as Zo moves in to congratulate you, you push her away for the moment, intent on getting in one more – not to impress her, but to prove to yourself that you have it down properly. After another few failed rotations, you complete another, much faster than the first. Like before, Zo steps into your space, her hands first grabbing onto your elbows before trailing down your forearms and ending at your own hands. She could take the scabbard from them... but, instead, she simply stands there and holds your hands for a moment. Her deep, emerald-green eyes stay locked onto yours as they turn into crescents underneath her proud, glowing smile. Her hands are very warm and soft against your own. Eventually, she pulls away, the scabbard back in her hands, and she sheathes the sword. That’s enough training for one day. |The remainder of your time training with Zo goes by smoothly and quickly. You’ve learned just about everything she can teach you, and at this point, it’s just a matter of refining it and utilizing different applications for your newfound balance and handling with your weapons. It’s not that you can swing harder or faster, and it’s not that you’ve learned a new method of parrying or anything like that; it’s simply that you have a better understanding of your weapon as a veritable extension of yourself, and now, you can move it as smoothly and as precisely as your arm or your leg. Zo has taught you to walk; you need to learn to run on your own time. [var0 |New Ability: Equanimity: when used in combat, all physical attacks have an additional 10% chance to critical hit. ] When it comes time to end your session with Zo, [zo.fucked |she steps into you, wrapping her arms around your body, holding you to her and nuzzling her nose into [pc.heightRange 0 72 999 |the nape of your neck |against the meat of your back ], enjoying the feel of your body against hers. She may be a monk, and she may not have a lot of material wants, but if there’s any one thing she does want right now, it’s for this moment with you to not end just yet. When you pull away from her, you give her a kiss on her lips, lingering for just a moment; a wordless promise that there will always be more later. She’s a monk; she knows how to be patient. |she steps into your space once more, hesitating at first, before reaching out with her hand and grasping onto yours. Your fingers interlock; she squeezes; and then, you two just... enjoy each other’s company for a time. Her face is pointed straight ahead, but her eyes are turned towards you, and a shy, coy smile faintly splays her lips. It’s a short distance – only about two dozen steps – from the little field in her grove to her [flags.ZO_UPGRADE 3|home|shack], but you walk with her, hand-in-hand, the whole way, and when you get to its door, she struggles with herself to let go. Her eyes are on your own; they travel from your eyes, to your [pc.feet], then back up. She looks over her shoulder, nibbling into her bottom lip, as she considers maybe inviting you in. rows.original: You ask Zo if you two could practice that game that you two had invented, where she throws rocks at you from one side of the field and you bat them away with that wooden weapon of hers from the other. It’s more than practicing your reflexes: you see the rocks before you watch them arc through the air, and that sort of intuition has more practical uses in your personal day-to-day life than playing games in the grass. Zo tilts her head to one side and frowns apologetically. She looks down at her stomach, her right hand rubbing the small bump on her tummy, then, with some regret, she shakes her head ‘no.’ She’s not comfortable performing that sort of training when she’s carrying your child. Just as you were about to suggest something else, she rests her hand on your chest; then, she puts her hands together at the palms, her fingers pointed towards you; then, she points her herself with her right index finger; then, she points towards both of her eyes with her index and middle fingers before pointing them towards you again. She’s suggesting that you can still do them yourself, and she can watch and teach; she just can’t perform them with you. Although it might feel like you’re missing something, that still works for you. You’ve mastered these techniques yourself by now anyway; it’s just a matter of refining what you know down until it’s second-nature to you, and that means doing them again and again and again.
rows.translation: 你问佐，你们俩能不能练习一下你们一起发明的那个游戏——就是她从场地的一边朝你扔石头，而你则用她给的那个木制武器把石头打掉。这可不仅仅是锻炼反应速度而已：你…… 看到 眼前的障碍 观看 那些弧线在空气中划过，而这种直觉在日常生活中其实比在草地上玩游戏要有用得多。 佐歪着头，带着歉意皱起了眉头。她低头看着自己的肚子，右手部轻轻抚摸着肚子上那个小凸起，然后，带着些许遗憾，她摇了摇头：“不行。当她怀着你的孩子时，进行那种类型的训练会让她感到很不自在。” 就在你准备提出其他建议的时候，她将手部放在你的胸前；然后，她把双手部的掌心相对，手部指朝你的方向；接着，她用右手部的食指指着自己；随后，她用食指和中指分别指向自己的两只眼睛，最后再次将这两根手部指指向你。 她是这个意思。 你 你仍然可以自己完成这些任务，而她可以观察并给予指导；只是她无法与你一起一起完成这些任务而已。 虽然你可能会觉得自己在错过某些东西，但实际上这种安排也是可行的。毕竟你现在已经掌握了这些技巧，剩下的就是不断练习，将所学的知识内化为自己的本能反应，而这就需要反复不断地练习才行。

rows.original: [var0 |The movement you’ve managed to learn from Zo and the unique weapon she’s learned has had some fairly dramatic results for you in battle. Whenever you think back to training with it, it’s almost as if your enemies move more slowly, and their actions are more predictable, allowing you to dodge swings and attacks you very much doubt you’d ever have evaded before you had trained with her. You still don’t see yourself using her weapons in combat, but, all the same, it never hurts to keep yourself sharp. You ask Zo if she’s willing to have another session with that unique weapon of hers. |Zo has a unique weapon that you’ve never seen before: a pair of short sticks, each about the size of her forearm, attached together by a rope at their ends, tethering them together in a single, long line. She can whip it around herself at blindingly fast speeds, which, while impressive, also means that they’re lightweight, so they wouldn’t carry a ton of force behind their swings. You don’t see yourself ever using a weapon like it in a real fight, but... well, all the same, there’s no such thing as being too informed. You ask Zo about that unique weapon of hers. You don’t plan on using one like it in combat, but you’re also curious if learning how to wield it can have other beneficial effects for you in a combative setting. ] [flags.ZO_BAB_RANDO |She nods once before bending down to pick up Vai, hooking her hands underneath his armpits, and taking him back into the [flags.ZO_UPGRADE 3|house|shack] – this practice in particular involves a lot of small, fast-moving objects, and not having a child nearby would go a long way, no matter how confident you two are in your capabilities. When she returns, she grabs you by your wrist, pulling you towards the field at the back of her grove, where she likes to practice. Once you two are standing in the center of the grassy field, she pulls out the weapon in question, tucked and hidden away by hooking it into the belt of her pants and draping her wide top overtop it – you doubt she goes anywhere without them, which, honestly, isn’t too weird, considering you do the same with your own [pc.weapon]. |She nods once and, enthusiastically, grabs you by your wrist, pulling you towards the field at the back of her grove, where she likes to practice. Once you two are standing in the center of the grassy field, she pulls out the weapon in question, [var1 |holding onto it by the rope, the sticks dangling and bumping into each other down by her knees. |tucked and hidden away by hooking it into the belt of her pants and draping her wide top overtop it – you doubt she goes anywhere without them, which, honestly, isn’t too weird, considering you do the same with your own [pc.weapon]. ] ] [zo.intuitionRange 0 1 2 3 |Now that you two are here, though, Zo takes a moment to consider what exactly to teach you when it comes to using a weapon like hers. She knows you aren’t looking to use it in combat, but even you can tell a person that swinging a sword around will, at the very least, improve hand-eye coordination (and build some muscles while you’re at it). Surely she can teach you something in a similar vein. After a moment, with her eyes cast to the ground as she contemplates, she bends at the knees and reaches into the grass, her fingers sifting through the wavy green blades and prodding at the dirt beneath. From it, she picks up a single pebble, perhaps a bit larger than her claw, and shows it to you, making sure you know exactly what it is she’s holding. Then, she tosses it into the air, and, on the way down, she swings her weapon at it – and the resounding clack! of the weapon hitting the pebble echoes throughout the grove, and the pebble flies off into some random direction. Before you think to ask her what the purpose of that was, Zo already has her hands in the grass, searching out another one. She finds four, and instead of tossing and hitting them all, one-by-one, she reaches for your hand; pours all four of them into your palm; closes your fingers into a fist; and then flicks her own fingers in a quick, snappy, throwing motion, before pointing to herself. Just to be clear, you ask her if she’s asking you to throw rocks at her. She nods, then steps ten paces away, her weapon at the ready: one stick in her hand, and the other tucked into her armpit, ready to swing as soon as you throw a rock. It’s certainly an unusual method of teaching[pc.isDK |, but, hell, you won’t deny that throwing rocks at someone can be fun[pc.corruptionRange 50 100 |... even if it’s less fun when they ask you to do it ] ]. You open softly, with an underhand toss, arcing the pebble through the air towards her. She swings at it, but the only sound you hear is the whiff of her weapon arcing through the open air – she’s missed entirely. Undeterred, she resumes her stance, and you underhand toss the second one. When she swings, you hear the clack! of her weapon striking true, followed by the sound of the pebble shooting through the air like an arrow. Already she’s prepared for the next, so you toss it underhanded again, and again, as soon as the pebble is in her weapon’s reach, she swings, and she strikes the rock into the grass between you two. You wonder to yourself if maybe you’re going a bit soft on her. You aren’t sure if you’d appreciate such kiddy-glove throws. You asked her for training, and you aren’t sure how much training she’s getting from hitting gently-arcing rocks moving at slow, arced speeds through the air. So, you reel your arm back, and you throw the last one as hard as you can, overhand and straight at her. You do indeed hear another clack! echo through the grove – and you see Zo lean her head back, recoiling from the strike. When she leans forward again, she removes her silver mask, her fingers gently rubbing at her forehead. You beaned her right in the face! Before you have the chance to apologize, though, Zo nods enthusiastically to you, her smile spreading infectiously across her lips, and she spins her index finger in a circle as she places her mask back on. She wants you to do it again. Well... okay. She asked. You start combing the grass from more pebbles. |It’s difficult to forget the kind of highly-unique training regimen that Zo put you through the last time you had asked for some practice with that weapon of hers. It was far more challenging than you had expected: it tested not only your comfort and proficiency with a weapon you could barely understand how to hold and swing, but also your hand-eye coordination far more than with a sword, and it also demanded that you take into account things like Zo’s body as she moved, to predict how fast or slow the rock moved, and what arc it would take as it went through the air, and when it’d be within striking distance. Best of all, on top of being strenuous, it’s also pretty fun. If you and Zo sat down to establish some rules and guidelines, you two could make a game out of this. Zo, having anticipated you asking for another session like the one before, took the liberty to gather up a pile of pebbles for you to stand by when you were away. Like before, she takes ten paces into the grassy field, before turning to face you, her weapon in her hand and at the ready when you are. Last time, you opened the session with a couple of easy, soft pitches, with high arcs and slow speeds, and when you ramped it up to full-blown overhand pitches, you wound up hitting her in the face. You aren’t going to go back to the soft throws – now that she’s experienced the full might of your throwing arm, it would be a disservice to her if you leaned back again – but you also aren’t going to open as hard as you can. You have to find a middle ground to start with. You scoop up a handful of the pebbles and keep them in your non-dominant hand, plucking them out individually with your fingers with your free hand to throw. You open with a quick, overhand toss, not too hard, not too light, and she swings at it easily, the clack! of the rock hitting her weapon echoing throughout the grove. The next two throws are met with the same, fluid, now-somewhat-practiced ease: she reads the language of your body; sees the arc of the rock before you throw it; and reacts to the throw before it happens. Even as you ramp up the strength of your throws, sending them cutting through the air faster and faster, Zo bats them all away, matching your pace and maintaining her composure. A wide grin’s spread across her lips after a few moments of you tossing rocks and her not missing a single one. She’s of a similar mind: it’s pretty fun! Still, this is training, and clearly, you’re being too soft on her. You dump all the remaining rocks into your dominant hand, shuffling them in your grip so that you can easily slide them from your palm to your thumb and forefinger. Then, you rear your hand back, and you start throwing them as quickly as you can, one by one. You’re losing a lot of strength with this method, but you hope to make up for it by overwhelming Zo with pebbles. A part of you hopes that she misses one. Even at your increased pace, Zo adapts by switching hands with the weapon after every swing: the half of the weapon that isn’t held swings right into her free hand, and she repeats the process, matching your throw for throw with her swing for swing. You make her really work for it, of course: her wrists have to twist and her eyes have to constantly flit from your body to the arcs of the rocks, and she stays on her toes to hit the ones that go high and to shift away from the ones that are aimed for her body. She doesn’t hit them all, and not all of the ones she does hit back are sent in your direction – she sidesteps a few here and there, and some of them bounce off her weapon and ricochet over her shoulder, or straight into the ground. By the time your hand is free of pebbles for you to throw, Zo is panting and out of breath... but her joyous smile has almost turned cocky with how large it is, and she’s ready for you to grab another fistful from her pile to start again. You’ll just have to start throwing them faster, you guess. |A topic that’s hovered in the back of your mind for the past little while is how you intend to trip up Zo in your unique training regimen with her. She’s gotten so good at reading your body and predicting the movement of the rocks as you throw them, even on the throws where you’re deliberately trying to obfuscate the movement of your arm, that she either hit every rock that she could back to you, or she dodged the ones that she couldn’t. On the one hand, that means that she’s gotten really good at this kind of practice, and maybe you should be proud of her and her skill – but, on the other, perhaps you aren’t giving her the practice she needs. Through all your pondering, you came up with just one possible solution... but it’s undeniably cheating. The only way you can do it fair and square is if you throw them faster. You also need to remember to aim for Zo, but not at her. The goal isn’t it hit her with a rock – it’s to make her swing and miss. Zo takes her position halfway out into the grassy little field in her grove, ready for another training session like before. In her right hand is one half of her unique weapon, with the other tucked into her armpit. The bulbous ends of her braided hair hover behind her head slightly, enough to produce slack in the lengths of her braids, and even from your distance, you can see the silvery shimmer of her eyes, ready to answer any swing you make with one of her own. You heft the handful of rocks. You aren’t going to whip out the one unfair move just yet – she needs to warm up to it. It isn’t like your throwing arm hasn’t been getting in some practice, anyway. As usual, you throw the rocks in Zo’s direction, one after the other, flexing your throwing arm to toss them harder and harder. And, as usual, Zo has a read on your every action and motion, and is able to counter every single rock, no matter how fast it’s moving or what arc it’s traveling in. You wonder how much of what she’s doing is her special vision that lets her see the world so differently and intuitively, or if she’s just got really good reflexes. By the time you’re halfway down the bunch of rocks in your hand, you decide – fuck it. It’s cheating, but you want to see how good Zo really is. You move all the rocks from your offhand to your main hand, similar to before, and you wind your fist back. But rather than throw them one by one as quickly as possible, you simply throw them all at once. Upwards of fifteen pebbles, all soaring through the air together, traveling in Zo’s general direction. How many will she hit? Will she step back to dodge them all? Will she silently berate you for pulling a dirty trick? You’re curious as could be. Zo, though... she stands at the ready as always, her weapon ready to swing with the flick of her wrist and the swing of her arm. Her reaction is hardly different from how she normally stands and swings at you. It’s like she knew from the beginning that you were going to do this. As the stones approach her, she swings her weapon, her arm flailing three times in front of her, and ending with the free half of the weapon tucked beneath her opposite armpit. You could make out the motion of her arm, but not of the weapon – it moved too quickly for you to track. But, what your eyes couldn’t see, your ears could hear: with all three swings, you heard the cacophonous claclaclaclaclaclaclaclaclaclaclaclaclaclaclack! of her countering every single pebble thrown at you. Not a single one made it past: all the rocks you threw are launched off at different angles, hurdling harmlessly into the grass around you and into the trees of the grove. Once the final stone rains down, Zo eases her stance, her weapon no longer at the ready, and the shimmering silver glow fades from her eyes. She smiles at you, but it’s not a cocksure, smug smile from having performed an impressive feat; it’s more of a friendly, ‘that was fun!’ kind of smile that a friend gives another after a close game. 当那些石头终于落下来之后，佐放松了她的姿态，手部中的武器也不再处于备战状态，她眼中那闪烁的银色轻型芒也渐渐消失了。她对你笑了笑，但那并不是那种因为完成了一项令人印象深刻的举动而表现出的自信满满、沾沾自喜的笑容，而更像是一种友好的、表示“刚才真有趣！”的微笑。那种朋友在一场激烈的比赛结束后彼此之间会露出的微笑。 她将武器折叠起来，用绳子固定好，然后把两根木制的枪杆放在手部掌上，递给你。现在轮到你了。 ]
rows.raw: " [var0 |The movement you’ve managed to learn from Zo and the unique weapon she’s learned has had some fairly dramatic results for you in battle. Whenever you think back to training with it, it’s almost as if your enemies move more slowly, and their actions are more predictable, allowing you to dodge swings and attacks you very much doubt you’d ever have evaded before you had trained with her. You still don’t see yourself using her weapons in combat, but, all the same, it never hurts to keep yourself sharp. You ask Zo if she’s willing to have another session with that unique weapon of hers. |Zo has a unique weapon that you’ve never seen before: a pair of short sticks, each about the size of her forearm, attached together by a rope at their ends, tethering them together in a single, long line. She can whip it around herself at blindingly fast speeds, which, while impressive, also means that they’re lightweight, so they wouldn’t carry a ton of force behind their swings. You don’t see yourself ever using a weapon like it in a real fight, but... well, all the same, there’s no such thing as being too informed. You ask Zo about that unique weapon of hers. You don’t plan on using one like it in combat, but you’re also curious if learning how to wield it can have other beneficial effects for you in a combative setting. ] [flags.ZO_BAB_RANDO |She nods once before bending down to pick up Vai, hooking her hands underneath his armpits, and taking him back into the [flags.ZO_UPGRADE 3|house|shack] – this practice in particular involves a lot of small, fast-moving objects, and not having a child nearby would go a long way, no matter how confident you two are in your capabilities. When she returns, she grabs you by your wrist, pulling you towards the field at the back of her grove, where she likes to practice. Once you two are standing in the center of the grassy field, she pulls out the weapon in question, tucked and hidden away by hooking it into the belt of her pants and draping her wide top overtop it – you doubt she goes anywhere without them, which, honestly, isn’t too weird, considering you do the same with your own [pc.weapon]. |She nods once and, enthusiastically, grabs you by your wrist, pulling you towards the field at the back of her grove, where she likes to practice. Once you two are standing in the center of the grassy field, she pulls out the weapon in question, [var1 |holding onto it by the rope, the sticks dangling and bumping into each other down by her knees. |tucked and hidden away by hooking it into the belt of her pants and draping her wide top overtop it – you doubt she goes anywhere without them, which, honestly, isn’t too weird, considering you do the same with your own [pc.weapon]. ] ] [zo.intuitionRange 0 1 2 3 |Now that you two are here, though, Zo takes a moment to consider what exactly to teach you when it comes to using a weapon like hers. She knows you aren’t looking to use it in combat, but even you can tell a person that swinging a sword around will, at the very least, improve hand-eye coordination (and build some muscles while you’re at it). Surely she can teach you something in a similar vein. After a moment, with her eyes cast to the ground as she contemplates, she bends at the knees and reaches into the grass, her fingers sifting through the wavy green blades and prodding at the dirt beneath. From it, she picks up a single pebble, perhaps a bit larger than her claw, and shows it to you, making sure you know exactly what it is she’s holding. Then, she tosses it into the air, and, on the way down, she swings her weapon at it – and the resounding clack! of the weapon hitting the pebble echoes throughout the grove, and the pebble flies off into some random direction. Before you think to ask her what the purpose of that was, Zo already has her hands in the grass, searching out another one. She finds four, and instead of tossing and hitting them all, one-by-one, she reaches for your hand; pours all four of them into your palm; closes your fingers into a fist; and then flicks her own fingers in a quick, snappy, throwing motion, before pointing to herself. Just to be clear, you ask her if she’s asking you to throw rocks at her. She nods, then steps ten paces away, her weapon at the ready: one stick in her hand, and the other tucked into her armpit, ready to swing as soon as you throw a rock. It’s certainly an unusual method of teaching[pc.isDK |, but, hell, you won’t deny that throwing rocks at someone can be fun[pc.corruptionRange 50 100 |... even if it’s less fun when they ask you to do it ] ]. You open softly, with an underhand toss, arcing the pebble through the air towards her. She swings at it, but the only sound you hear is the whiff of her weapon arcing through the open air – she’s missed entirely. Undeterred, she resumes her stance, and you underhand toss the second one. When she swings, you hear the clack! of her weapon striking true, followed by the sound of the pebble shooting through the air like an arrow. Already she’s prepared for the next, so you toss it underhanded again, and again, as soon as the pebble is in her weapon’s reach, she swings, and she strikes the rock into the grass between you two. You wonder to yourself if maybe you’re going a bit soft on her. You aren’t sure if you’d appreciate such kiddy-glove throws. You asked her for training, and you aren’t sure how much training she’s getting from hitting gently-arcing rocks moving at slow, arced speeds through the air. So, you reel your arm back, and you throw the last one as hard as you can, overhand and straight at her. You do indeed hear another clack! echo through the grove – and you see Zo lean her head back, recoiling from the strike. When she leans forward again, she removes her silver mask, her fingers gently rubbing at her forehead. You beaned her right in the face! Before you have the chance to apologize, though, Zo nods enthusiastically to you, her smile spreading infectiously across her lips, and she spins her index finger in a circle as she places her mask back on. She wants you to do it again. Well... okay. She asked. You start combing the grass from more pebbles. |It’s difficult to forget the kind of highly-unique training regimen that Zo put you through the last time you had asked for some practice with that weapon of hers. It was far more challenging than you had expected: it tested not only your comfort and proficiency with a weapon you could barely understand how to hold and swing, but also your hand-eye coordination far more than with a sword, and it also demanded that you take into account things like Zo’s body as she moved, to predict how fast or slow the rock moved, and what arc it would take as it went through the air, and when it’d be within striking distance. Best of all, on top of being strenuous, it’s also pretty fun. If you and Zo sat down to establish some rules and guidelines, you two could make a game out of this. Zo, having anticipated you asking for another session like the one before, took the liberty to gather up a pile of pebbles for you to stand by when you were away. Like before, she takes ten paces into the grassy field, before turning to face you, her weapon in her hand and at the ready when you are. Last time, you opened the session with a couple of easy, soft pitches, with high arcs and slow speeds, and when you ramped it up to full-blown overhand pitches, you wound up hitting her in the face. You aren’t going to go back to the soft throws – now that she’s experienced the full might of your throwing arm, it would be a disservice to her if you leaned back again – but you also aren’t going to open as hard as you can. You have to find a middle ground to start with. You scoop up a handful of the pebbles and keep them in your non-dominant hand, plucking them out individually with your fingers with your free hand to throw. You open with a quick, overhand toss, not too hard, not too light, and she swings at it easily, the clack! of the rock hitting her weapon echoing throughout the grove. The next two throws are met with the same, fluid, now-somewhat-practiced ease: she reads the language of your body; sees the arc of the rock before you throw it; and reacts to the throw before it happens. Even as you ramp up the strength of your throws, sending them cutting through the air faster and faster, Zo bats them all away, matching your pace and maintaining her composure. A wide grin’s spread across her lips after a few moments of you tossing rocks and her not missing a single one. She’s of a similar mind: it’s pretty fun! Still, this is training, and clearly, you’re being too soft on her. You dump all the remaining rocks into your dominant hand, shuffling them in your grip so that you can easily slide them from your palm to your thumb and forefinger. Then, you rear your hand back, and you start throwing them as quickly as you can, one by one. You’re losing a lot of strength with this method, but you hope to make up for it by overwhelming Zo with pebbles. A part of you hopes that she misses one. Even at your increased pace, Zo adapts by switching hands with the weapon after every swing: the half of the weapon that isn’t held swings right into her free hand, and she repeats the process, matching your throw for throw with her swing for swing. You make her really work for it, of course: her wrists have to twist and her eyes have to constantly flit from your body to the arcs of the rocks, and she stays on her toes to hit the ones that go high and to shift away from the ones that are aimed for her body. She doesn’t hit them all, and not all of the ones she does hit back are sent in your direction – she sidesteps a few here and there, and some of them bounce off her weapon and ricochet over her shoulder, or straight into the ground. By the time your hand is free of pebbles for you to throw, Zo is panting and out of breath... but her joyous smile has almost turned cocky with how large it is, and she’s ready for you to grab another fistful from her pile to start again. You’ll just have to start throwing them faster, you guess. |A topic that’s hovered in the back of your mind for the past little while is how you intend to trip up Zo in your unique training regimen with her. She’s gotten so good at reading your body and predicting the movement of the rocks as you throw them, even on the throws where you’re deliberately trying to obfuscate the movement of your arm, that she either hit every rock that she could back to you, or she dodged the ones that she couldn’t. On the one hand, that means that she’s gotten really good at this kind of practice, and maybe you should be proud of her and her skill – but, on the other, perhaps you aren’t giving her the practice she needs. Through all your pondering, you came up with just one possible solution... but it’s undeniably cheating. The only way you can do it fair and square is if you throw them faster. You also need to remember to aim for Zo, but not at her. The goal isn’t it hit her with a rock – it’s to make her swing and miss. Zo takes her position halfway out into the grassy little field in her grove, ready for another training session like before. In her right hand is one half of her unique weapon, with the other tucked into her armpit. The bulbous ends of her braided hair hover behind her head slightly, enough to produce slack in the lengths of her braids, and even from your distance, you can see the silvery shimmer of her eyes, ready to answer any swing you make with one of her own. You heft the handful of rocks. You aren’t going to whip out the one unfair move just yet – she needs to warm up to it. It isn’t like your throwing arm hasn’t been getting in some practice, anyway. As usual, you throw the rocks in Zo’s direction, one after the other, flexing your throwing arm to toss them harder and harder. And, as usual, Zo has a read on your every action and motion, and is able to counter every single rock, no matter how fast it’s moving or what arc it’s traveling in. You wonder how much of what she’s doing is her special vision that lets her see the world so differently and intuitively, or if she’s just got really good reflexes. By the time you’re halfway down the bunch of rocks in your hand, you decide – fuck it. It’s cheating, but you want to see how good Zo really is. You move all the rocks from your offhand to your main hand, similar to before, and you wind your fist back. But rather than throw them one by one as quickly as possible, you simply throw them all at once. Upwards of fifteen pebbles, all soaring through the air together, traveling in Zo’s general direction. How many will she hit? Will she step back to dodge them all? Will she silently berate you for pulling a dirty trick? You’re curious as could be. Zo, though... she stands at the ready as always, her weapon ready to swing with the flick of her wrist and the swing of her arm. Her reaction is hardly different from how she normally stands and swings at you. It’s like she knew from the beginning that you were going to do this. As the stones approach her, she swings her weapon, her arm flailing three times in front of her, and ending with the free half of the weapon tucked beneath her opposite armpit. You could make out the motion of her arm, but not of the weapon – it moved too quickly for you to track. But, what your eyes couldn’t see, your ears could hear: with all three swings, you heard the cacophonous claclaclaclaclaclaclaclaclaclaclaclaclaclaclack! of her countering every single pebble thrown at you. Not a single one made it past: all the rocks you threw are launched off at different angles, hurdling harmlessly into the grass around you and into the trees of the grove. Once the final stone rains down, Zo eases her stance, her weapon no longer at the ready, and the shimmering silver glow fades from her eyes. She smiles at you, but it’s not a cocksure, smug smile from having performed an impressive feat; it’s more of a friendly, ‘that was fun!’ kind of smile that a friend gives another after a close game. She folds her weapon at the rope and lays both of the wooden shafts across her palms, extending it to you. rows.original: [zo.intuitionRange 0 1 2 3 |All too soon, it’s your turn to take the weapon and try to bat back the stones as Zo throws them at you. You hardly even know how to hold the [pc.isDK |damn |silly ] thing, much less swing it effectively and hit a rock the size of your fingernails back at her. Still, you asked her to teach you, and this is how she decided to do it. Perhaps the best method of teaching something so alien to you is learning to run before you walk. You stand where she stood, holding one end of the two-piece weapon and letting the other loosely hang by its end next to your [pc.leg]. You windmill it a few times, trying to get a feel for its reach and its weight and balance; you swing it once, feeling the loose end hammer its way through the air in front of you. It’s an unwieldy weapon for what you’re used to, but you saw how Zo could use it, and how quickly she could swing with it. Clearly it has some merit. You rear your arm back, tense and ready for Zo to throw. You narrow your eyes on her, ready to try and react to her movement– Zo shakes her head and steps into you, putting her hand on your arm and pushing down, instructing you to ease up. She’s unable to articulate her lesson, so, instead, she runs both of her hands along your arm, from wrist to shoulder, soothingly rubbing and massaging at your muscles and sinews with her fingers. It’s rather relaxing, [pc.libidoRange 0 50 |but, knowing that you’re trying to train, she’s probably trying to teach you something |and you start thinking that, if you guide her hands a bit, she could probably relax something else that’s getting more and more tense with her hands ]. Changing it up a bit, Zo holds your wrist with one hand, keeping your arm steady, as she runs her other over it, from your forearm to your shoulder. It’s not a massage, and the motion feels very deliberate. It’s like she’s trying to smooth you out, like your arm was a sheet and she’s ironing out the crinkles. Then, after a moment of that, she points her fore- and middle fingers at your eyes; then, she points at herself, at her forehead; then, she shakes her head and motions to the ground. After that, she points at both of your eyes again; then, points to your forehead. It’s difficult to parse. Try not to tense your arm. Remain calm and smooth – ‘fluid’ might be a better word. Don’t watch her, but, also, don’t watch... anything in particular. Something about your eyes and your forehead? You tell her that you aren’t certain that you understand, but you’re willing to try anyway. It’s good enough for her, and she goes back to where she was, the pebbles back in her hand. Don’t tense. Stay calm. One fluid motion. But what are you supposed to be watching for? Zo throws the rock towards you the same way you threw them to her: underhanded, gently, with a clear and soft arc through the air. She specifically told you not to watch her, so you didn’t, but the rock is too small to clearly make out in the air between you two. When you swing, you whiff, and it probably wasn’t close. She doesn’t approach you again, though, so your form must not have been incorrect. Stay calm. One fluid motion. When Zo swings her arm in another underhanded toss, your eyes aren’t necessarily on her and her form, but towards her. You see her move and you see her arm swing, and you see the moment she lets the pebble fly, but you don’t watch any of it – the information enters your mind, and you do nothing with it. When the stone comes within swinging distance of your weapon, you swing vertically, aiming to slam the pebble into the ground. You hear less of a ‘clack’ and hear more of a click! as the edge of your weapon grazes the stone out of the air. It doesn’t so much ‘slam into the ground’ as it does awkwardly tumble off at a different angle, thrown out of position by the glancing blow. But you hit it. You aren’t sure how, but you did. It’s a short order and a few more underhanded tosses before Zo is out of pebbles to throw. You’ve hit maybe less than half of the stones she threw – but, considering you barely understood what she was trying to teach, and you’re unfamiliar with her weapon, it’s a good deal more than you were hoping for. She steps into your space and holds her hands out for you to return her weapon. That’s enough training for one day. |Okay, so, Zo just demonstrated that she’s... pretty good at this method of training. Her hand-eye coordination with the weapon of hers is a league above your own, having trained with it for most of her life and you first held it last time you did this training, so she has that going for her, but even with the tools you’re most comfortable with – hell, even with your bare hands – it’d be a stretch to compare her intuition to yours. No, stop it. That’s not what this training is about; of course you’re not going to compare favorably to her. It’s about your own self-improvement. You hold the weapon in your hand exactly as you had last time: your fingers loosely gripping one end, with the other dangling by its rope down by your [pc.leg]. The last time you did this training, you managed to finish by knocking away maybe less than half of the stones she threw at you, but you nonetheless made considerable progress: it was less about the literal arc and motion of the rock as it cut through the air, and more about Zo’s body language and the motions she made as she threw it. It was about discerning her intent – over- or under-handed; the speed; whether she was going to fake you out – and interpreting and responding to it accordingly. It’s not the rock you’re focusing on or even the body of the person throwing it: it’s the unspoken language that goes into throwing it. Zo patiently waits for your go-ahead before she starts throwing rocks at you. Once you’re ready, you get into your stance from last time: calm and ready, your eyes in her direction, but not on her. When she plucks a pebble from the mound beside her, she rears her arm backward, and throws it at you overhanded, but with far less strength than you know she’s capable of. It’s not the rock that you watch, and it’s not the swing of her arm. It’s all information that you subconsciously take in, but you don’t consciously process. The angle of her wrist; the speed of her arm; the twist of her hips; the lunge of her legs– The rock is too small for you to accurately track through the air, but nonetheless, you swing the weapon horizontally, not at where you guess the rock to be, but where you understand it to be. You hear the echoing clack! of the weapon hitting the pebble out of the air, and you feel the vibration of the two colliding shoot up through your hand. It was a solid, strong hit. You don’t see where the pebble flies off to, though. Zo nods enthusiastically, her grin spreading across her lips, cheek-to-cheek. Whatever it is you’re doing and understanding, it’s exactly what she was hoping for. She’s already wrist-deep back into the mound of pebbles, pulling them out by the fistful, ready to continue your training with her. You allow yourself a moment of pride at having apparently figured it out, but you don’t hold onto it for long. Zo’s already rearing her hand back once more. This training session is only going to get more intense. |You doubt you’ll be able to accomplish what Zo just did, especially today. The most you can hope to do, and the most you can honestly ask of yourself, is just keeping up your pace. It’s not a very humble thing to say, but you’ve been making lots of progress, and while you still aren’t confident enough in wielding Zo’s weapon to consider using it in a battle, you still– Zo doesn’t give you her two-piece weapon to practice with, and instead places the weapon into the belt of her outfit, the two wooden prongs dug into the fabric securely. Instead, she retrieves your [pc.weapon] and presents it to you across both her open palms. She wants you to practice with something your more familiar with this time. Gingerly, you take it from her, feeling its familiar heft in your hands. Despite being far more comfortable with it than with whatever Zo’s weapon is, you can’t help but still feel a bit... awkward with it, in the context of your training. Perhaps that’s the next step of the lesson: now that you understand the basics, it’s time to apply it to a weapon you’re actually going to use in a fight. You stand in the grassy field, your [pc.weapon] at the ready, as she takes her own position beside the mound of pebbles. Performing this training requires a certain mindset, a different way of seeing Zo and the way she moves her body. It’d be easy if you could do that life-energy-vision-thing that she showed you when you two first met, but, you’ll have to settle for your eyes. When Zo throws the first rock at you – overhanded, not as strong as it could be, but not exactly weak or slow – you knock it from the air without so much as a thought in your head. You had expected your muscle memory to be thrown off by using such a wildly different tool, but it was like your body wasn’t the muscle that you were training this whole time. You read Zo’s intent, and you responded appropriately. The weapon in your hand was ancillary to knowing how she was moving and reacting to it. Zo, doing what you did with her, places all her pebbles into her throwing hand, and throws them at you one-by-one as quickly as she can spin her shoulder, sliding the next pebble into place between her thumb and forefinger. It’s a bit more intense than batting them back one-by-one, but, as before, you respond to each toss correctly and perfectly, hitting them out of the air as they come to you. You don’t even see most of the rocks, and you aren’t watching Zo’s body so much as you’re ‘reading’ it with every toss. When you consciously try to hit a rock out of the air, you realize that it requires far more effort and precision than if you just kept doing what you were doing. As one final test, Zo splits the last few remaining rocks between her two hands evenly, and rears both of her arms back, intent on throwing them both at once. She isn’t ambidextrous, and that much momentum and force on both sides of the body is going to knock it off-kilter, meaning your reading of her motion is skewed– But, nonetheless, with one swing of the [pc.weapon], you hear the repetitive, rapid-fire clicks of the stone against it. While it wasn’t quite as impressive as Zo’s feat of speed and intuition, you’ve proven that you’ve nonetheless mastered Zo’s teaching, and now, it’s just a matter of honing it. [var0 |New Ability: Intuition: when used in combat, Evasion is increased by an additional 15%. ] With that last throw, Zo has no more rocks to throw in her hands, and getting any more would just belabor the point. [zo.fucked |She walks toward you, a certain sashay in her hips as she does, and her lips constantly shift between smiling with genuine joy and appreciation for you as her student, and smiling like a lover that knows she’s about to get some. You set your [pc.weapon] down for the moment, and when she closes into you, she places her hands on [pc.heightRange 0 72 999 |your shoulders |your hips ], introducing herself into your personal space. Her eyes are narrowed on your own, and her nose is [pc.heightRange 0 72 |against yours |pressed into your collar ]. There’s a lot to be happy about right now: Zo’s proven to you that she’s an excellent teacher even with her disability, and you’ve proven to Zo that you’re the best student a monk could ask for. rows.raw: " [zo.intuitionRange 0 1 2 3 |All too soon, it’s your turn to take the weapon and try to bat back the stones as Zo throws them at you. You hardly even know how to hold the [pc.isDK |damn |silly ] thing, much less swing it effectively and hit a rock the size of your fingernails back at her. Still, you asked her to teach you, and this is how she decided to do it. Perhaps the best method of teaching something so alien to you is learning to run before you walk. You stand where she stood, holding one end of the two-piece weapon and letting the other loosely hang by its end next to your [pc.leg]. You windmill it a few times, trying to get a feel for its reach and its weight and balance; you swing it once, feeling the loose end hammer its way through the air in front of you. It’s an unwieldy weapon for what you’re used to, but you saw how Zo could use it, and how quickly she could swing with it. Clearly it has some merit. You rear your arm back, tense and ready for Zo to throw. You narrow your eyes on her, ready to try and react to her movement– Zo shakes her head and steps into you, putting her hand on your arm and pushing down, instructing you to ease up. She’s unable to articulate her lesson, so, instead, she runs both of her hands along your arm, from wrist to shoulder, soothingly rubbing and massaging at your muscles and sinews with her fingers. It’s rather relaxing, [pc.libidoRange 0 50 |but, knowing that you’re trying to train, she’s probably trying to teach you something |and you start thinking that, if you guide her hands a bit, she could probably relax something else that’s getting more and more tense with her hands ]. Changing it up a bit, Zo holds your wrist with one hand, keeping your arm steady, as she runs her other over it, from your forearm to your shoulder. It’s not a massage, and the motion feels very deliberate. It’s like she’s trying to smooth you out, like your arm was a sheet and she’s ironing out the crinkles. Then, after a moment of that, she points her fore- and middle fingers at your eyes; then, she points at herself, at her forehead; then, she shakes her head and motions to the ground. After that, she points at both of your eyes again; then, points to your forehead. It’s difficult to parse. Try not to tense your arm. Remain calm and smooth – ‘fluid’ might be a better word. Don’t watch her, but, also, don’t watch... anything in particular. Something about your eyes and your forehead? You tell her that you aren’t certain that you understand, but you’re willing to try anyway. It’s good enough for her, and she goes back to where she was, the pebbles back in her hand. Don’t tense. Stay calm. One fluid motion. But what are you supposed to be watching for? Zo throws the rock towards you the same way you threw them to her: underhanded, gently, with a clear and soft arc through the air. She specifically told you not to watch her, so you didn’t, but the rock is too small to clearly make out in the air between you two. When you swing, you whiff, and it probably wasn’t close. She doesn’t approach you again, though, so your form must not have been incorrect. Stay calm. One fluid motion. When Zo swings her arm in another underhanded toss, your eyes aren’t necessarily on her and her form, but towards her. You see her move and you see her arm swing, and you see the moment she lets the pebble fly, but you don’t watch any of it – the information enters your mind, and you do nothing with it. When the stone comes within swinging distance of your weapon, you swing vertically, aiming to slam the pebble into the ground. You hear less of a ‘clack’ and hear more of a click! as the edge of your weapon grazes the stone out of the air. It doesn’t so much ‘slam into the ground’ as it does awkwardly tumble off at a different angle, thrown out of position by the glancing blow. But you hit it. You aren’t sure how, but you did. It’s a short order and a few more underhanded tosses before Zo is out of pebbles to throw. You’ve hit maybe less than half of the stones she threw – but, considering you barely understood what she was trying to teach, and you’re unfamiliar with her weapon, it’s a good deal more than you were hoping for. She steps into your space and holds her hands out for you to return her weapon. That’s enough training for one day. |Okay, so, Zo just demonstrated that she’s... pretty good at this method of training. Her hand-eye coordination with the weapon of hers is a league above your own, having trained with it for most of her life and you first held it last time you did this training, so she has that going for her, but even with the tools you’re most comfortable with – hell, even with your bare hands – it’d be a stretch to compare her intuition to yours. No, stop it. That’s not what this training is about; of course you’re not going to compare favorably to her. It’s about your own self-improvement. You hold the weapon in your hand exactly as you had last time: your fingers loosely gripping one end, with the other dangling by its rope down by your [pc.leg]. The last time you did this training, you managed to finish by knocking away maybe less than half of the stones she threw at you, but you nonetheless made considerable progress: it was less about the literal arc and motion of the rock as it cut through the air, and more about Zo’s body language and the motions she made as she threw it. It was about discerning her intent – over- or under-handed; the speed; whether she was going to fake you out – and interpreting and responding to it accordingly. It’s not the rock you’re focusing on or even the body of the person throwing it: it’s the unspoken language that goes into throwing it. Zo patiently waits for your go-ahead before she starts throwing rocks at you. Once you’re ready, you get into your stance from last time: calm and ready, your eyes in her direction, but not on her. When she plucks a pebble from the mound beside her, she rears her arm backward, and throws it at you overhanded, but with far less strength than you know she’s capable of. It’s not the rock that you watch, and it’s not the swing of her arm. It’s all information that you subconsciously take in, but you don’t consciously process. The angle of her wrist; the speed of her arm; the twist of her hips; the lunge of her legs– The rock is too small for you to accurately track through the air, but nonetheless, you swing the weapon horizontally, not at where you guess the rock to be, but where you understand it to be. You hear the echoing clack! of the weapon hitting the pebble out of the air, and you feel the vibration of the two colliding shoot up through your hand. It was a solid, strong hit. rows.translation: [zo.influenceRange 0 1 2 3 |你呆呆地望着那些灌木丛，试图弄明白她究竟是怎么做到的。她只是把手指放在灌木的枝条上，然后那些枝条就……自动为她让开了道路。就好像她只是礼貌地请求了一下，那些植物就乖乖地服从了。你究竟该如何模仿这种行为呢？你既不能向她请教，甚至也不能让她给你任何提示。 接下来的几分钟里，你都在绞尽脑汁，试图弄清楚她究竟是怎么做到的…… 灌木丛 要听从她的命令。你收集到的其他浆果都很容易获取，这意味着你几乎没有机会去尝试模仿……她之前为你做过的那些事情。 但也许问题就出在这里：你想得太多了。 在佐的教诲与实践中，她的行事方式从来都不容易用逻辑来理解。显然，这并不像轻轻按在木头上就能让它移动那么简单——每当她做出什么举动，无论是让木头弯曲变形，还是治愈伤口，这些行为都离不开她那种神秘的能量，正是这种能量让她那束编成的头发在身后飘动。 是强迫它弯曲，还是通过说服、请求，又或是其他方式？无论采用哪种方法，要让木头乖乖地弯曲到所需的位置，都需要投入同样的精力与专注力。而学会如何让木头弯曲而不使其折断，其实就是朝着“用思想治愈伤痛”这一目标又迈进了一步。 在那一排灌木的尽头，还有一簇浆果。它们紧紧地挂在细茎上，被另一根茂密的树枝挡住了，因此想要摘到它们确实有些困难，但也不是完全不可能或令人沮丧。如果你无法让那根茎弯曲，至少也不用让佐来帮你完成这个任务了。 你将手指放在那根挡住你的树枝上，集中注意力观察它，试图模仿佐之前所做的动作。 [var1|你对自己试图做的事情其实了解甚少，也缺乏真正的认识：除了在初次遇见佐时，她曾帮你治愈那道刀伤，以及有那么一次她让你从动态的角度了解了宇宙的真正面貌之外，你对其所做的事情以及实现这些事情的方法，也只是略知一二而已。不过，哪怕只是“略知一二”，总比一无所知要好吧……毕竟，每个人都不可能一开始就什么都知道……|你拥有 一些 了解佐是如何利用某些方法取得那些成果的，你也知道，通过更多的训练，自己同样有能力释放出那样的潜力。但这就让人不禁思考：自己所掌握的这些有限知识，是否真的能够帮助自己实现目标呢？不过，至少你现在拥有的知识总比一无所有要好，所以这已经是一个良好的开始了……] 究竟应该关注什么，其实是一件相当模糊的事情。你需要在自己内心深处寻找，寻找那股“本质”——也就是当佐向你展示宇宙的能量时，你所看到的那股力量。你必须把握住它，并将其应用到这种植物的本质之中，想办法让它们相互融合，甚至产生共鸣，这样这种植物才会为你让路。 上次佐这样做的时候，完成后她还得把那些树枝重新放回原来的位置。所以，你总觉得自己拥有正确的思维方式，即使执行方式可能还不太对。但你怎么才能确定自己真正理解了自己的本质呢？ 还是灌木丛的？如果你…… 做 如何让他们结合在一起呢？你该怎样“表达”自己的想法呢？ 佐跪坐在你身旁，耐心地等待着你做出你所能做的任何事情。但尽管你已经尽了最大努力，那株灌木最多也只是让它的叶子在风中摇摆，发出嘈杂的沙沙声而已。 那根树枝依然牢牢地、固执地留在原地。 佐将手部放在你的肩上，用无声的动作告诉你：目前的训练已经足够了。显然，确实是这样。 [pc.isDK |令人沮丧的 |令人失望 ] 不得不让这件事以一个不太理想的结果收场；你明明能够如此清晰地想象自己的目标以及实现它的方法，但却始终无法跨越最后那道小小的障碍。在真正宣称“任务完成”之前，你至少应该像自己曾经承诺的那样，努力去抓住最后那些机会，哪怕这意味着要费一番周折。 当你站起来的时候，你的思绪会被这一课以及自己为何没有完成它所困扰，但你内心某个无意识的层面却会注意到：在这个被天然屏障环绕的树林里，风竟然出奇地静止着。... |最后一个苹果离地太高了，根本够不着。 [pc.heightRange 0 72 | |哪怕是像那样高大的人也是如此。 ]你可以通过站立或者跳跃来达到通常能够触及的高度。[pc.hasWings |你或许不应该通过使用自己的方式来作弊。 [pc.wings] ]无论她做了什么，这些行为都与她那神秘的能量有关。 [pc.isDK |胡说八道 |训练 ]你也需要运用同样的方法。 上次你做类似的事情时，从那丛灌木上采摘浆果，你觉得自己取得了一些进展，但就在你真正有所成就之前，Zo打断了你。 那种你已经取得的成就感，以及那种你觉得自己即将达到的领悟，从那以后就一直萦绕在你的脑海中。这种感觉就像漂浮在记忆的深处，你一直试图留住它，这样就能从你停下的地方继续前进。 现在正是最好的时机…… 在内心深处寻找那种存在于你以及世界上所有生物与植物身上的“本质”。这并不是要跳得非常高；而是要用你的这种本质去与他人相连接，将其与他人的本质融合在一起，从而让它们能够“进行交流”。但是，你究竟在试图接触什么？如果你…… 做 当你终于找到了自己一直在寻找的东西，接下来你会怎么做呢？你该如何与那棵树、那片大地、那阵风沟通，告诉它们你真正需要什么？ [var1|你到底想去哪里？ 开始吗？|至少有一件事是明确的：你至少知道自己应该从哪里开始，但接下来该往哪个方向前进呢？] 你闭上眼睛，绷紧双腿，屈膝降低重心。很可能并不是风将佐推向了那么高的地方；如果她不是依靠自己的力量跳得那么高，那么她一定是与大地产生了某种共鸣，从而获得了向上的力量。 |虽然这听起来既愚蠢又不切实际，但你自己已经看到了这些成果，而正是为了取得这些成果，你才来到了这里。你努力让自己保持清醒的头脑——既然注定要显得像个傻瓜，那还不如干脆把这件事做到底。 |你甚至都不确定自己这样做是否真的能达成什么目的，反而只会显得很愚蠢，但幸运的是，Zo肯定不会把这件事告诉别人。你不妨试着保持清醒的头脑，把这件事坚持做完吧。 ] 在那一瞬间的紧张之后，当你积蓄起足部部的力量，准备向地面冲刺——至少你是这么感觉的——你突然向上跃起，将体内所有的力量都释放了出来。 [pc.legs]然后你猛地向上跳跃，将所有那些你之前储存起来的“能量”都释放到了地面。 而，正如预料的那样，你什么也没达到。你的跳跃高度并没有比之前高任何一点。
